procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 54 of 1964. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, altered the conviction of the respondent to one under Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.), and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years and a fine of Rs. 1,000 (with a default sentence of six months rigorous imprisonment). It also ordered that Rs. 500 of the fine, if realized, be paid as compensation to the child.

issue.issue_text: Whether the act of causing injury to the vagina of a seven-and-a-half-month-old child by fingering constitutes an offence under Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code (assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty).

facts: The accused caused injury to the vagina of a seven-and-a-half-month-old female child by fingering.
The lower courts and a majority in the High Court had held that this was not an offence under Section 354 because a child of that age is incapable of having a developed sense of modesty.
law: Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code punishes assault or criminal force on a woman with the intent to outrage her modesty.
Section 10 of the Indian Penal Code defines a "woman" as a female human being of any age.
The Supreme Court defined the "essence of a woman's modesty is her sex."
The Court established that modesty is an objective attribute that a female possesses from birth, regardless of her age, intelligence, or state of consciousness (e.g., sleeping, under anesthesia).
application: The Court rejected the view that modesty is a subjective feeling or a developed sense of shame that the victim must personally experience. If that were the case, assaults on sleeping, unconscious, or very young victims would not be covered.
The focus of the offence is on the "culpable intention of the accused," not the reaction of the victim.
The Court determined that any act done to a woman that is "clearly suggestive of sex according to the common notions of mankind" falls under the mischief of Section 354.

In this case, the accused's deliberate act of interfering with the infant's vagina was inherently sexual in nature. This act, combined with the surrounding circumstances, demonstrated his intent to outrage the modesty which is an attribute of her sex.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the act of causing injury to the infant's vagina by fingering did constitute an offence under Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code. The Court reasoned that modesty is an inherent attribute of a female's sex from birth, and the offence is determined by the accused's intent and the sexual nature of the act, not by the victim's age or her subjective feeling of being outraged.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the act of causing injury to the vagina of a seven-and-a-half-month-old child by fingering constitutes an offence under Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code (assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty).
appellant_arguments: When construing Section 354 of the IPC, it is irrelevant to consider the age, physical condition, or the subjective attitude of the woman against whom the assault has been committed or the criminal force used.
respondent_arguments: The subjective reaction of the woman is a relevant factor in determining if her modesty was outraged.
In construing Section 354, the age, physical condition, and subjective attitude of the woman against whom the assault was committed are relevant considerations.
A female child of seven and a half months does not have a sense of modesty, and therefore, her modesty cannot be outraged.

The placement of Section 354 in the chapter of the Penal Code dealing with offences affecting the human body, and not in the chapter dealing with offences relating to decency and morals, supports the view that the victim must have a subjective sense of modesty.

cases.case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax v. Express Newspapers Ltd.
cases.principle: The heads of income in s. 6 of the Income-tax Act are mutually exclusive. An income falling under one head cannot be put under another head if it escapes taxation under the computing section corresponding to the former head.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The argument that the reaction of the woman concerned decides whether an offense has been committed is fallacious. Furthermore, the interpretation of the section should not be determined by its placement within a specific chapter of the penal code, such as the one on offenses affecting the human body versus the one on decency and morals.
obiter: The reported decisions on the question to which our attention was drawn do not furnish clear assistance.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the offence of outraging modesty under Section 354 IPC is determined by the accused's intent and the nature of the act, not the victim's subjective reaction or understanding. Modesty is an inherent attribute of a female, regardless of her age. Therefore, the respondent's deliberate act of fingering and causing injury to the vagina of a seven-and-a-half-month-old child was an act from which the intention to outrage her modesty must be inferred, making him punishable under the section.
legal_tests_applied: The test of the outrage of modesty must, therefore. be whether a reasonable man will think that the act of the offender was intended to or was known to he likely to outrage the modesty of the woman. In considering the question. he must imagine the woman to be a reasonable woman and keep in view all circumstances concerning her. such as. her station and way of life and the known notions of modesty of such a woman.
policy_considerations: These offences are not only offences against the individual but against public morals and society as well, and that object can be achieved only if the word "modesty" is considered to be an attribute of a human female irrespective of fact whether the female concerned has developed enough understanding as to appreciate the nature of the act or to realise that it is offensive to decent female behaviour or sense of propriety concerning the relations of a famale with others.
